questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'DNA as the Genetic Material' refers to.
questions.a: Three classic experiments crowned DNA as the hereditary molecule: Griffith's 1928 heat-killed smooth pneumococci passed a 'transforming principle' to harmless rough cells, Avery, MacLeod and McCarty wiped the principle out only with DNase, and Hershey and Chase watched radioactive phosphorus - not sulfur-labelled protein - ride into E. coli inside T2 phages.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'DNA as the Genetic Material'.
questions.a: Whoever destroys DNA destroys the transforming ability, and only the phage's DNA enters the host - so DNA, not protein, carries heredity.

questions.q: Under which section is 'DNA as the Genetic Material' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 7.1 (source: kebt107.txt sections 7.1.1-7.1.3, Figs. 7.1-7.3)

concepts.title: Gene Packaging in Prokaryotes and Eukaryotes

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Gene Packaging in Prokaryotes and Eukaryotes' refers to.
questions.a: Bacteria squeeze one circular chromosome into a nucleoid by negative supercoiling helped by histone-like proteins, while eukaryotes wind linear DNA around histone octamers of H2A, H2B, H3 and H4 into beads-on-string nucleosomes with a single H1 holding the linker, then coil 10 nm fibres through 30 nm and 300 nm stages to 700 nm metaphase chromosomes.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Gene Packaging in Prokaryotes and Eukaryotes'.
questions.a: Supercoiling packs the bacterial loop; histone spools and progressive folding tuck metres of eukaryotic DNA into a nucleus.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Gene Packaging in Prokaryotes and Eukaryotes' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 7.2 (source: kebt107.txt section 7.2, Figs. 7.4-7.8)

concepts.title: Genome Size Units and the Coding Fraction

questions.q: Using the method 'Genome Size Units and the Coding Fraction', work with: bp_total = 150. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of coding_share.
questions.a: 0 as a fraction

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Genome Size Units and the Coding Fraction' and work with: bp_total = 24. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of coding_share.
questions.a: 0 as a fraction

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Genome Size Units and the Coding Fraction' refers to.
questions.a: Genome sizes run from a few thousand bases in viruses to billions in mammals, and the reading convention chains them - a thousand base pairs make one kilobase and a thousand kilobases one megabase; the three-billion-base human genome carries over twenty thousand protein-coding genes that fill only about two percent of it, the rest being repetitive and other non-coding DNA.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Genome Size Units and the Coding Fraction'.
questions.a: Divide bases by a thousand for kilobases and again for megabases; multiply the megabase total by the coding percent to size the gene share.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Genome Size Units and the Coding Fraction', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: kb_value = bp_total / 1000

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Semi-Conservative Replication Machinery' refers to.
questions.a: Each daughter duplex keeps one parental strand and gains one new complement - the semi-conservative rule that Messelson and Stahl proved with heavy nitrogen and caesium chloride gradients; helicase unzips the fork, primase lays 10-12 nucleotide RNA primers, DNA polymerase III extends only 5' to 3', the lagging side is built in 1000-2000 nucleotide Okazaki pieces, polymerase I swaps primers for DNA, and ligase seals the nicks.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Semi-Conservative Replication Machinery'.
questions.a: One old strand plus one new strand per duplex, a continuous leading side and a discontinuous lagging side make replication semi-discontinuous.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Semi-Conservative Replication Machinery' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 7.3 (source: kebt107.txt sections 7.3.1-7.3.4, Figs. 7.9-7.16)

concepts.title: Bacterial Division Timing and Culture Growth

questions.q: Using the method 'Bacterial Division Timing and Culture Growth', work with: elapsed_min = 300, starter_cells = 300. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of cells_after.
questions.a: 9830400 units

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Bacterial Division Timing and Culture Growth' and work with: elapsed_min = 75, starter_cells = 75. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of cells_after.
Explain in your own words what 'Bacterial Division Timing and Culture Growth' refers to.
questions.a: E. coli doubles every twenty minutes, so the generation count of an experiment is simply the elapsed minutes divided by twenty, and the culture size follows a doubling ladder from the starting cells.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Bacterial Division Timing and Culture Growth'.
questions.a: Divide the minutes by twenty for generations, then double the starter culture once per generation.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Bacterial Division Timing and Culture Growth', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: generations = elapsed_min / 20

questions.q: Using the method 'Genetic Code Triplet Arithmetic', work with: amino_acids = 100, bases_per_codon = 5, stop_codons = 25. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of with_stop.
questions.a: 303 units

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Genetic Code Triplet Arithmetic' and work with: amino_acids = 150, bases_per_codon = 20, stop_codons = 400. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of with_stop.
questions.a: 453 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Genetic Code Triplet Arithmetic' refers to.
questions.a: Gamow's counting settled the code's design: one base gives only four options and a pair sixteen - too few for twenty amino acids - but a three-base code offers sixty-four codons; sixty-one of them specify amino acids, the remaining three are stops, AUG doubles as the start signal, and Nirenberg's poly-U decoded the first word, UUU for phenylalanine.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Genetic Code Triplet Arithmetic'.
questions.a: Four raised to the codon length counts the code; subtract the three stops for the sense codons.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Genetic Code Triplet Arithmetic', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: codons_total = 4 ** bases_per_codon

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Transcription, mRNA Processing and Translation' refers to.
questions.a: RNA polymerase reads a promoter with its Pribnow box, unwinds about seventeen base pairs and strings ribonucleotides at roughly forty per second until a terminator - with sigma leaving after initiation and rho sometimes ending the run; eukaryotic transcripts then gain a methyl-G cap and a poly-A tail and lose their introns by splicing, before ribosomes translate the message codon by codon from charged tRNAs until a release factor meets a stop codon.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Transcription, mRNA Processing and Translation'.
questions.a: Copy only the gene into RNA, dress and trim the eukaryotic transcript, then let tRNAs and the wobble rule translate it at the ribosome.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Transcription, mRNA Processing and Translation' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 7.4-7.6 (source: kebt107.txt sections 7.4.1-7.6, Figs. 7.20-7.32)

concepts.title: Gene Mutation and DNA Repair Arithmetic

questions.q: Using the method 'Gene Mutation and DNA Repair Arithmetic', work with: cut_downstream = 24, cut_upstream = 60. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of excised_length.
questions.a: 84 units

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Gene Mutation and DNA Repair Arithmetic' and work with: cut_downstream = 15, cut_upstream = 12. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of excised_length.
questions.a: 27 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Gene Mutation and DNA Repair Arithmetic' refers to.
questions.a: Mutations come as additions, deletions and substitutions - purine-for-purine changes are transitions while purine-for-pyrimidine swaps are transversions, and tautomeric shifts or base analogs like 5-bromouracil sneak such swaps past replication; cells answer with base excision repair through glycosylase-made AP sites, nucleotide excision repair that cuts out UV-induced T-T dimers by clipping upstream and downstream, and mismatch repair led by Mut proteins.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Gene Mutation and DNA Repair Arithmetic'.
questions.a: Add the two cut distances around a lesion to size the patch that excision repair must refill.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Gene Mutation and DNA Repair Arithmetic', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: excised_length = upstream_cut + downstream_cut
